patent: Filed in the US on 1923-02-06 (German priority 1922-02-11) and issued 1928-01-24 to Arthur Scherbius of Berlin, the German electrical engineer who invented the Enigma rotor cipher machine; the patent was assigned to Chiffriermaschinen Aktiengesellschaft, the Berlin firm that sold the Enigma. The ciphering core shown is a rotor machine: a keyboard feeds cables of one wire per letter (26 in the example) through a stack of drums whose two faces are cross-wired in scrambled order, the drums advance after every letter, and in the embodiment the output drives a telegraph tape perforator. The text presents that core as already proposed. What is claimed is the group-length device: a counter driven with the drums cuts the supply after a set number of letters, so sender and receiver can mark and re-check group boundaries and a lost letter in transmission does not desynchronize the rest of the message; a hand lever then lets clear text be sent without advancing the drums. There is no reflector, the part that made later Enigma machines self-reciprocal; deciphering here needs the current passed the other way through the drums or the input and output cables interchanged.

figs.1: General arrangement, drawn sideways on the sheet; shown upright here. Key board 1 (bottom right, broken away to show the key contacts) feeds cable 3 to drum 4; the drum stack on shaft 5 reads, left to right, stationary drum 10, sliding drum 4, cipher drums 6, 7, 8, 9 and stationary drum 11; cables 13 and 14 from drums 10 and 11 run to perforator 12 (right). The fifth row of letters on drums 6 to 9 reads n, i, a, g, the example key word; the drum alphabets omit j. Stepping train: armature 25 of magnet 26 carries blade-spring 24, which pawls ratchet teeth 23 on driving wheel 15 (seen edge-on); spur wheel 18 drives gears 16 and 17 on shafts 19 and 20, whose gears 21 and 22 mesh with toothed crowns of drums 6 and 8 (only these two couplings are drawn). Counter 39 (top left, reading 0013999) is geared to wheel 15; sliding contacts 40 to 44 and switches 45 to 49 select which figure disks gate the supply. Lever 27 shifts drum 4 and carries plate 29 with contacts 30 and 31; with contacts 32 and 33, lever 35 on stud 34, and blade spring 36 caught by groove 37 and nose 38 of the armature, it restarts the machine after a stop and keeps the counter out of circuit until the next letter. + and − mark the supply poles.
figs.2: End face of one cipher drum (drum 6), seen along the shaft. The ring of small circles is the contacts on that face; the dash-dot chords show the scrambled internal wiring that joins each contact to a contact on the opposite face. Only some of the connections are drawn.
figs.3: The same drum seen from the side, axis horizontal. Contact pins stand out on both end faces; the serrated band at one end is the toothed crown that the stepping gear drives. The crossing dash-dot lines are the internal wires between the two faces.

parts.4: Slides along shaft 5 but does not turn. Spring 28 holds it against drum 6 (ciphered path to the perforator through drums 6 to 9, drum 11 and cable 14); depressing lever 27 pushes it against drum 10 (clear path through cable 13).
parts.10: Keyed to the shaft and carries pins on its inner face only; it is the clear-text path to the perforator.
parts.11: Keyed to the shaft and carries pins on its inner face only; it is the ciphered-text path to the perforator.
parts.12: Each type lever is driven by its own electromagnet; the text names a magnetic perforator of the Wheatstone type.
parts.24: Acts as the pawl of the ratchet formed with teeth 23; each release of armature 25 advances wheel 15 by one tooth.
parts.38: The text once writes "armature 38" for the contact kept by spring 36; elsewhere 38 is the nose behind groove 37 on armature 25.
parts.39: The drawing shows the counter at 13999, the state described just before the 14000th letter stops the machine.

glossary.def: A rotor: a wheel with a contact on each face for every letter, the two faces wired together in a fixed scrambled permutation; turning it changes the substitution.
The starting letter positions of the drums, set by hand from the letters on their rims; both machines must start from the same setting.
A keyboard-driven punch that records Morse signals as holes in paper tape; the tape is then run through an automatic telegraph transmitter. Wheatstone's system was the standard one.
Punched paper tape for submarine-cable or line telegraphy.
A toothed wheel advanced one tooth at a time by a spring finger (the pawl); here blade-spring 24 on the armature drives teeth 23.
The numbered wheels of the counter (units, tens, hundreds and so on).
The supply circuit fed from the source of current.
Through one or more intermediate transfers of ownership before reaching the named assignee.
